To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

age differences in fluid aspects of cognition are associated with a reduction in the number of simultaneously activated nodes in a network, the maximum allowable node activation, or the speed of propagating activation.

the number of simultaneously available nodes in an associative memory is reduced with age, that this reduction accounts for age differences in a variety of tasks that require memory search, and that this reduction is not due to a general reduction of the number of nodes in long-term storage.
older adults have a smaller maximum number of simultaneously active cognitive processes, and a slower rate of activation between nodes, than do young adults.

understanding the mechanisms underlying age-related differences in cognitive functioning, particularly in relation to fluid abilities.
the development of a theory of cognitive aging that will provide a coherent framework for the interpretation of age-related changes in cognition.

the field is in a state of flux.

we have developed an initial model of cognitive aging that is consistent with a wide variety of cognitive aging phenomena, that is based on explicit mechanisms that can be investigated empirically, and that provides a plausible account of one of the more intractable problems in cognitive aging research.

formal models can provide a useful framework for organizing the knowledge base in cognitive aging, and can help to identify important areas of research that have not yet been explored.
